t: Introduction: topic, aim and plan
n: In this lecture we consider the concept and types of euthanasia, palliative medicine and hospices. These are the ethical and legal aspects of medical care at the end of life. The plan: the history and types of euthanasia, their legal assessment, the attitude of religions, palliative care, hospices, and ethical problems in oncology. The main idea: at the terminal stage what matters is not prolonging life but relieving pain and suffering and improving the quality of the remaining life. In 1983 the World Medical Association adopted the Declaration of Venice on terminal illness. It defines the duties of the physician.

t: The term “euthanasia” and F. Bacon
n: The term “euthanasia” was proposed in the seventeenth century by the English philosopher F. Bacon. From the Greek “eu”, good, and “thanatos”, death, that is, an easy and gentle death. In 1623 Bacon wrote: the physician's duty, along with restoring health, is to relieve the suffering of the illness. Even when there is no hope, death should be more peaceful. Euthanasia in Bacon's interpretation is close to the present-day concept of palliative care: the essence is relieving the suffering of a person doomed to die. Attention: today euthanasia is understood in the narrow sense, only active and passive. This differs from Bacon's meaning.

t: Attitudes to the elderly and sick in antiquity
n: In antiquity, among some peoples, dying of illness or old age was considered unacceptable. Ancient religions and customs did not forbid this but, on the contrary, approved it. The reasons: the limited possibilities of medicine and scarcity of food. Examples: on the island of Keos the elderly drank poison, that is, hemlock, and poisoned themselves. In Japan frail old people were carried to Mount Obasuteyama. Among the Eskimos the old people went off into the tundra themselves and froze to death.

t: Sparta, epidemics and the causes of suicide
n: According to Plutarch, in Sparta the fate of a newborn depended on the elders. The father brought the child to them, and they examined it. A healthy child was returned to its father. Weak and deformed children were thrown into a chasm, since their lives were considered useless. The child was tested by bathing it in wine. During a plague epidemic, patients who were bound to die were burned together with the corpses. Thousands of infants who had contracted poliomyelitis were buried alive or left without care. Durkheim: in antiquity, among the causes of suicide, old age and illness were leading. The functional view brought forth a “culture of death” and eugenic measures.

t: The Hippocratic Oath and contemporaries
n: In the Hippocratic Oath the physician promises not to give a deadly drug when asked and not to point the way to obtaining it. Some of his contemporaries, however, considered it natural and beneficial for the life of weak, hopeless patients to end with an “easy death”. That is, the thinkers of antiquity were not of one mind, and their opinions were not the same. Attention, there is a risk of error: Hippocrates and his contemporaries did not hold one opinion.

t: Case analysis: ancient customs
n: Case analysis. On the island of Keos the elderly drank poison, that is, hemlock. Elderly Japanese were carried to Mount Obasuteyama. The Eskimos went off into the tundra to freeze to death. In ancient religions and customs such cases were not forbidden but approved. The reasons: the limited possibilities of medicine and shortage of food. Today euthanasia in many of its manifestations is judged to be contrary to the basic principles of medical ethics. Question: can these customs be justified if food and medical help are sufficient? Why?

t: A.F. Koni: conditions for active euthanasia
n: The Russian jurist A.F. Koni considered active euthanasia possible only as an exception, when four conditions are met. First condition: the conscious and firm demand of the patient. Second: the impossibility of relieving the suffering by existing methods. Third: a consilium must prove that life cannot be saved. Fourth: the law-enforcement authorities must be warned in advance.

t: Declarations on euthanasia: 1980 and 1987
n: On the declarations on euthanasia. In 1980 the Roman Catholic Church adopted the “Declaration on Euthanasia”. The World Medical Association, that is, the WMA, adopted such a declaration at its Madrid Assembly in 1987. The exception in the Madrid Declaration is this: respect for the wish not to obstruct natural death at the terminal stage is not an exception to this rule. Remember the dates: the Catholic Church's declaration, 1980; the WMA's Madrid Declaration, 1987.

t: Arguments of supporters and opponents of euthanasia
n: Arguments of supporters and opponents of euthanasia. Supporters: a person should have the right to choose to continue or to end his life. Those close to him are freed from the suffering, while quality of life in suffering declines. Opponents: life is the highest and inviolable value, and euthanasia is contrary to the essence of medical practice. Opponents warn: legalisation creates a risk of abuse, which is called the “slippery slope”.

t: Euthanasia: the logic of “against” and “for”
n: The logic of “against” and “for” on euthanasia. The “against” argument: the deliberate killing of an innocent person is always a moral evil; euthanasia is the deliberate killing of an innocent person, and therefore a moral evil. It is contrary to humanity and to the aim of medicine. The first basis of the “for” argument: the condition of some people is such that they are better dead than alive, for example in severe pain. The second basis: helping to improve someone's condition is always morally permissible. This argument has a serious flaw: it does not prove that the condition of all patients will really be improved, that is, it cannot be generalised.

t: Quick question and Attention: broad and narrow sense
n: Attention! Bacon's definition is in the broad sense, while the documents of the Catholic Church and the WMA are in the narrow sense: only active and passive euthanasia. Now quick questions. First question: who proposed the term “euthanasia”, in which century, and what does it mean? Second question: to which present-day concept is Bacon's interpretation close, and what is its essence? Third question: how is euthanasia understood in the declarations adopted by the Catholic Church in 1980 and by the WMA in Madrid in 1987?

t: Clinical death and the criterion of death
n: Clinical death is a reversible terminal state on the border between life and death; it lasts 5 to 6 minutes, sometimes less. The reversibility of clinical death requires the physician to treat it as a condition needing emergency care. In the modern understanding the criterion of death is necrosis of the brain: in brain death the person's autonomy and individuality are lost. The formation of resuscitation science in the 1960s and 70s changed the traditional criteria of death and opened the “zone of uncertainty” of which Yudin spoke. The table also notes Mukhin's insufflation of air into the lungs in 1805.

t: Types of euthanasia: an overview
n: An overview of the types of euthanasia. In the broad sense four types are distinguished: active, passive, or orthothanasia, medicothanasia and dysthanasia. Active euthanasia is divided into direct, that is, voluntary or involuntary, and indirect. Passive euthanasia, that is, orthothanasia, may be complete or partial. Thus the classification in the broad sense consists of active, passive, medicothanasia and dysthanasia.

t: Active euthanasia: the voluntary type and PAS
n: Active euthanasia is relieving torment by hastening death. It is also called the “filled syringe” method. Voluntary active euthanasia presupposes the patient's consent. If the patient carries it out himself, in the legal sense it is assessed as suicide. Sometimes suicide is carried out with the help of a physician. For this the term PAS arose, that is, physician-assisted suicide. WMA statement of 1992: PAS is contrary to ethical norms and must be condemned. The patient's right to refuse medical help, however, is respected.

t: The three forms of active euthanasia
n: Active euthanasia has three forms. Active euthanasia, that is, the “filled syringe method”, is the administration of a drug that leads to death; euthanasia leads only to deliberate death. The first form: “mercy killing”, which occurs when the physician cannot otherwise remove the suffering of a hopeless patient. The second: suicide with the physician's help, in which the physician helps an incurable patient end his life. The third: it can be done without a physician, the patient himself activating the appropriate device.

t: The examples of Kevorkian and Freud
n: The examples of Kevorkian and Freud. Jack Kevorkian is a former pathologist from the state of Michigan, USA. In 1990 to 1999, 131 patients committed suicide with his help. Several attempts were made to bring him to criminal liability, but without success. Only in 1999 was he charged with murder and sentenced. In 1939 Freud was diagnosed with cancer of the bowel. On 21 September he asked a friend to end his life; after two days of hesitation Dr Schur gave morphine. Assessment: according to the WMA statement of 1992, physician-assisted suicide is contrary to morality. The patient's right to refuse treatment, however, is respected.

t: The laws of the Netherlands and Spain
n: The laws of the Netherlands and Spain. In 2000 the Netherlands became the first country in the world to officially recognise active euthanasia. The Spanish parliament legalised euthanasia in 2021. It is also legalised in Belgium, Luxembourg, Colombia and some states of America. In the Netherlands the patient states his decision in sound mind, close relatives must agree, an independent physician also confirms, and it is carried out with the participation of law-enforcement officers. In Spain the patient must be over 18 and apply officially, the application is submitted twice with an interval of 15 days, the physician may refuse, and it is carried out by the physician or by the patient himself with assistance.

t: Involuntary active euthanasia: real cases
n: Attention: hastening death without the patient's consent, that is, involuntary active euthanasia, differs from the voluntary type and is judged in law as murder. In England the physician Harold Shipman, under the pretext of taking blood, injected a narcotic substance into a vein and caused the deaths of about 300 people, mainly elderly women; this is in the commission's conclusion, 2000. In 2006 a court in the state of New Jersey found the paramedic Charles Cullen guilty of killing 29 patients. He said he killed out of pity for the patients. During COVID-19 in Italy, Carlo Mosca killed two seriously ill patients to free up beds; in a clinic in Essen, too, two patients were given a lethal drug.

t: Euthanasia and eugenics: Hitler's programme
n: Euthanasia and eugenics: Hitler's programme. Eugenics is a scientific trend that arose in the first half of the twentieth century: improving the characteristics of the human population. Positive eugenics develops favourable qualities, while negative eugenics advocates eliminating the inferior. The stages of the programme: first came the idea of Binding and Hoche. On 1 September 1939 Hitler signed a secret order on euthanasia of “forms of life unworthy of life”. The aim then shifted to the “racial”. In August 1941 the programme was halted. The tribunal found it to be a crime against humanity.

t: Case analysis: voluntary or involuntary?
n: Case analysis: voluntary or involuntary? Active euthanasia carried out at the request of relatives, even if the patient cannot express his will, is assessed as involuntary euthanasia. The surgeon Yudin, while operating on his colleague Prof. Dieterichs, found incurable stomach cancer. At his wife's request he gave instructions to increase the anaesthetic. The former French Minister of Health Bernard Kouchner admitted that he had applied euthanasia to the severely wounded in the wars in Lebanon and Vietnam. Question: classify these three cases according to whether the patient's own consent is present or absent. Voluntary active euthanasia presupposes the patient's consent.

t: Indirect active euthanasia
n: In indirect active euthanasia, actions aimed at relieving suffering cause death. Usually analgesics are given in a large dose. Legal assessment: “causing death by negligence” under the Criminal Code of the Republic of Uzbekistan, or an “accident”. For this reason future physicians must know the principles and rules of palliative therapy. Attention: indirect is not the same as direct. In the direct type the aim is to hasten death; in the indirect the aim is to relieve suffering.

t: Passive euthanasia (orthothanasia)
n: Passive euthanasia, that is, orthothanasia, may be complete or partial. In the complete case, measures sustaining the life of a hopeless, severely suffering patient are abandoned; in the partial case, to a lesser extent. After the consilium records the fact of death, there is no need to continue resuscitation. In Doletsky's view, the struggle is justified only if there is hope of rescue. Attention: in brain death, even if circulation and breathing are artificially maintained, a person cannot be considered alive. This state becomes a source of meaningless suffering for those close to him. The personality is determined by the activity of the cerebral cortex. When the brain cells have died, the work of other organs loses meaning.

t: Legal assessment of orthothanasia: NTBR and DNR
n: Legal assessment of orthothanasia. In law, orthothanasia is regarded as a punishable act: Articles 116 and 117 of the Criminal Code may apply. Assessment: “improper performance of professional duties” or “leaving in danger”. By order of Nisden hospital, resuscitation is forbidden in malignant tumours and chronic diseases of the respiratory system and kidneys. There are two kinds of notation. NTBR is written in the case history in an English hospital and means “not for resuscitation”. DNR is written on a plaque on the bed in American hospitals and means “do not resuscitate”.

t: Examples of passive euthanasia and diagnostic errors
n: Examples of passive euthanasia and diagnostic errors. The former US President Richard Nixon, in a written appeal to physicians, asked that his life not be prolonged artificially if he became unable to express his will. Mitterrand, on a physician's advice, made a will and stopped his medication; McCain died in August 2018, having stopped medication a few days earlier. Petrarch breathed again a few hours before burial and lived another 30 years; the surgeon Bergmann refused to operate because of “incurable cancer”, but the tumour proved benign. In seriously ill patients serious errors of diagnosis and prognosis are possible; this is an important argument of opponents of euthanasia.

t: Laws: California, Indiana, Finland
n: A comparison of laws. In the state of Indiana the wish not to prolong life artificially in a severe incurable disease is formalised as a will. The California law, 1977, was called the “right to die” law and was aimed at stopping resuscitation; it was never once used, because a psychiatrist's opinion and the participation of a physician were obligatory. The association of psychiatrists forbade its members to take part; the medical association also forbade physicians. In Finland passive euthanasia exists, and stopping is not regarded as unlawful.

t: Limited resources: Pirogov and the Seattle committee
n: When resources are limited, the problem of choice arises. There is a shortage of apparatus or places: whom should be saved first? A committee decides, and the criterion becomes who is “more valuable”. Examples: in triage Pirogov set apart the hopelessly wounded; they were looked after mainly by a priest and a nurse. At the “Artificial Kidney” centre in Seattle, the queue for haemodialysis was determined by a committee of a physician, a lawyer and a religious figure. In 2020, during the coronavirus pandemic, COVID-19, a “death commission” was formed at a hospital in Texas.

t: Religious confessions and euthanasia
n: Religious confessions and euthanasia. Islam, Christianity and Judaism firmly oppose active and passive euthanasia. For them human life is sacred and inviolable: neither the patient himself nor the physician has the right to infringe upon it. In Buddhism the approach is different. The aim of life lies outside it, that is, in nirvana; renouncing life is considered an “exemplary” state. In Buddhism suicide occurs as an ordinary religious tradition, and the methods depend on the era and school.

t: Case analysis: whose turn is it?
n: Case analysis. In 1961 an article in “Life” magazine aroused debate about the “Artificial Kidney” centre in Seattle: the new apparatus was scarce and not enough for all patients. Usually the indication for a procedure is determined by the physician alone. Here, however, a committee was formed of a physician, a lawyer, a psychologist, and representatives of religion and the public. Questions: an elderly film star or a teenager? A successful businessman or a housewife with many children? A local politician or a wealthy immigrant? The press called the committee the “God committee”. In 2020, during COVID-19, a “death commission” was also formed in Texas.

t: Quick question, Attention and Remember
n: Attention: active euthanasia, passive euthanasia and medicothanasia are not the same. Active hastens death, passive abandons measures that sustain life, medicothanasia treats suffering. Remember: A-P-M-D, active, passive, medicothanasia, dysthanasia. The first two are regarded as euthanasia in the narrow sense. A broader classification: active, that is, direct voluntary and involuntary, and indirect; passive, that is, complete and partial; medicothanasia; dysthanasia. Quick questions: first, in which type is there the “filled syringe” method? Second, what does DNR mean? Third, which type is not contrary to law?

t: Medicothanasia and dysthanasia
n: Medicothanasia relieves suffering; failing to give help leads to legal liability. Its methods are conservative and symptomatic treatment; it is not contrary to ethics and law. Dysthanasia is the prolongation of life by radical methods, using extraordinary methods of treatment; it does not conflict with law and morality. The term was introduced by Savitsky in 1976. Three arguments for dysthanasia: life is the highest value; medicine develops; a “hopeless” patient sometimes recovers. In Izzat Sultan's drama “Iman” the later healing of a condition judged incurable is described.

t: The concept of palliative care
n: Palliative care is given to an incurable patient at the terminal stage. The term comes from the Latin “pallio”, meaning to cloak, to soften. It is a complex of medical, social and psychological help. It relieves pain and other suffering and is aimed at the maximum improvement of quality of life. The aim is to achieve the best quality of life for the patient and his family. Life is affirmed, and death is accepted as a natural process. Attention: palliative care neither hastens nor postpones death. In this it differs from active euthanasia, which hastens death.

t: The 1989 WHO statement and the Declaration of Venice
n: Documents on palliative care. The committee of the WHO, that is, the World Health Organization, stated in 1989 that a palliative programme should be developed instead of euthanasia. The WMA, that is, the World Medical Association, adopted the Declaration of Venice in 1983. According to it, the physician, having the patient's interests in mind, must relieve suffering as far as possible even in an incurable disease.

t: The Declaration of Venice: transplantation and opioids
n: The Declaration of Venice also speaks of transplantation and opioids. If the law does not forbid, a physician may artificially maintain the vital functions of the deceased in order to transplant organs; he must not be dependent on the recipient. WMA statement of 1990: patients with chronic pain who are doomed to die may be given non-opioid and opioid analgesics. Governments must ensure this. In practice, dying patients are more often helped by general practitioners. Therefore they must know palliative therapy. Quick question: on whom must the physician not depend when vital functions are maintained for the purpose of obtaining organs?

t: History of hospices
n: History of hospices. In the Middle Ages in Europe, places where exhausted, ailing pilgrims rested and recovered were called hospices. In 1842 in Lyon, France, the first hospice was opened for cancer patients. In 1947 the Cicely Saunders hospice was organised in London; in it, alongside medical procedures, psychological help was given to the patient. In 1967 St Christopher's Hospice opened in London. In 1975 the journalist Victor Zorza lost his daughter to cancer and conducted a campaign for hospices in the USA.

t: Principles and tasks of the hospice
n: A hospice is not a house of death: the aim is to ensure quality of life up to the last moment. Just as no charge is made for birth, none is made for death: help in hospices is given free of charge. The main tasks: reducing pain and fear, monitoring and symptomatic treatment, psychological help for the patient and those close to him, and psychosocial adaptation. Attention: death can be neither hastened nor slowed. This is the fundamental difference from euthanasia.

t: Admission to a hospice and hospices in Uzbekistan
n: Admission to a hospice is made in the following cases: home treatment is ineffective, the procedure cannot be performed at home, or those close to the patient need a short rest. In Uzbekistan the hospice service consists of several links. A mobile team gives help at home and advises the physician. Palliative departments are in oncology institutions, with 20 beds. The 2019 resolution of the Cabinet of Ministers is aimed at developing oncological care and hospices; hospices are in Tashkent, Samarkand, Fergana and Urgench. Interregional hospices, as independent institutions, give help in-patient and out-patient; they have 50 beds, and there is a methodological centre in Tashkent.

t: Ethical problems in oncology and the patient's stages
n: Ethical problems in oncology. Cancer is a strong stress for the patient and the family. Making the diagnosis and treatment give rise to fear and ethical problems. The patient's psyche may pass through six stages: from shock to acceptance of the disease. The first stage is shock, the second denial and withdrawal, the third aggression and search for a cause, the fourth psychological depression, the fifth and sixth struggle with fate and acceptance. The physician calms the patient, prepares him psychologically for treatment and strengthens faith in recovery.

t: Kübler-Ross: the five stages of a patient close to death
n: Elisabeth Kübler-Ross, in talking with dying patients, wrote the book “On Death and Dying”; in 1969 it was the best-selling book in the USA. Her idea: death is expressed by five stages through which the patient passes; the last is acceptance. The first stage is denial: “no, not me”. The second is anger: “why me?” The third is bargaining: “not now”, “a little longer”. The fourth is depression. The fifth is acceptance, in which the patient's emotional and mental state changes radically. The physician's responsibility: to ensure that the last days of the patient's life pass without fear and suffering, with respect.

t: Case analysis: telling a cancer patient the diagnosis
n: Case analysis. A patient with stomach cancer asks for his diagnosis. The physician chooses an approach taking into account the stage of the disease, the patient's age, occupation and cultural environment. According to the source, the physician may say “stomach ulcer” or “polyp”; in the documents “organic disease” is written, and the words “cancer” and “metastasis” are avoided. Attention: do not discuss the X-ray and the results of special examinations in the patient's presence; documents confirming the diagnosis must not fall into his hands.

t: Conclusion and review questions
n: Let us conclude. The types of euthanasia: active, that is, direct voluntary and involuntary, and indirect; passive, that is, orthothanasia, complete and partial; medicothanasia and dysthanasia. Legal assessment: voluntary active euthanasia is suicide, involuntary is murder; indirect is a consequence of negligence; medicothanasia is not contrary to morality and law. Palliative care neither hastens nor postpones death. The WMA Declaration of Venice, 1983, places on the physician the relief of suffering. A hospice is not a house of death but ensures quality of life; help is free of charge. An independent question: what are the main tasks of hospices?
